en: Your father became a sovereign;
If you challenge the judgment he received,
You will be maimed—
God has struck you senseless.
Yesterday, when our handful of Muslims
Waged a holy campaign against Beijing,
Your father, Khan Köksö, died;
My father Almambet
Died there as a martyr.
The pride of the forty warriors—
Mighty Chubak—died there too,
And many champions died beside them.
Semetey, your own cousin,
Do not incur his wrath—heed my words!
Such is the custom; this is my word—
Let Khan Semetey understand.
Crossing the lands of Ach-Maral and Merki,
Passing over the Ayry-Kaykang ridge,
The famed Keng-Kol and great Talas
Are not lands for you to besiege.
Semetey, son of the bloodthirsty hero—
Do not test my khanly uncle’s mettle;
You will lose your honor for nothing.
These are not people you can intimidate.
Let not your pretentious khanship
Be revealed for what it is right here.
If you provoke him,
He may slaughter every one of you,
Not sparing so much as a hair.
He may slaughter all of you,
Young and old alike, leaving none.
Let your wise men not act rashly,
For if your leader is a fool,
What fault lies with all the people?
Let the surviving Kazakhs
Not be forced to flee back to Sary-Arka.
Your people, champions, and khans—
As if another massacre had fallen upon you,
You will all be slaughtered.
If the bloodthirsty hero runs wild,
Can the combined right and left wings withstand him?
When that fierce warrior grows wrathful,
Does anyone who fights him escape alive?
Do not squander your own wealth,
O Kazakh people swollen with arrogance;
Do not let your blessed men be slaughtered
And then return home, all of you pleading,
Your heroes disgraced as cowards!
If war should break out by mischance,
And we meet spear against spear,
If by mischance we slaughter one another
And innocent people die,
If every district is devastated,
And we despair of precious life,
If the flower of the great nation,
The innocent people, are slaughtered,
Let us not share in such wickedness.
If the famous rumors prove true,
May He show no savagery,
And on the doomsday of resurrection
May He not make black donkeys of us.
May the smiting God not strike us;
May this handful of faithful people
Not stand on Judgment Day’s narrow path
Demanding their blood from us.
May He show no brutality
By killing the innocent,
And may He not humiliate the two of us,
Turn us into black donkeys, and ride us.
Understand what I have said;
Without quarreling or raising strife,
My noble cousin, heed my words!
I have a vessel upon the water,
One who can restrain obstinate speech:
Your mother’s own sister,
My unfortunate mother Kanykey.
Let us go to my valiant, ill-fated mother,
To Kanykey,
And place the matter before her.
Let us gather every elder capable of counsel,
Everyone with ears willing to listen,
Leaving no one out.
Let us seek and find a solution,
And reason the matter through.
Without insulting or quarreling,
Let us remain on good terms.”
So Külchoro
Offered words of wisdom.
But Ümötöy grew furious—
Now God had struck the khan senseless.
Like a prince commanding a nation,
Like one about to overturn everything,
He stiffened in anger—
Now God had struck the hero senseless.
The only son of brave Köksö—
Now God had struck the champion senseless.
As though his father Köksö had died
Because magnanimous Manas
Had simply handed him over to the Chinese,
As though he were chasing down
The last straggling foal of the ruined Kazakhs,
The wretch swaggered and smirked,
As though scattering plunder from a saddlebag.
The black slave strutted about,
As though carrying off his rightful share.
The scoundrel was going mad,
As though scattering plunder of silver coins.
Stiff with fury,
Ümötöy no longer behaved like a khan.
Though noble Choro implored him,
He refused and blocked his way.
If left to Ümötöy’s will,
He would reap and gather them
And stuff them into his pocket.
He would grind Talas to dust,
Cut down and topple its trees,
Engulf it utterly with his army,
And push down all its houses.
If the Kyrgyz were left to his will,
He meant to reap and gather them,
Leaving not one of them behind,
And heap them on his threshing floor.
Slaughtering their fleeting lives,
Ümötöy would simply mow them down.
His hair bristling wildly,
He shouted in anger,
Calling his Kazakhs
To thrust their raiding spears.
Looking across Talas,
A crimson haze rose like a mountain;
Ümötöy and his Kazakhs
Had become foes worse than the Chinese.
A black cloud rose like a mountain;
With Ümötöy bent on enmity,
They had become foes worse than the Kalmyks.
If left unhindered,
He seemed ready to slaughter the people as he passed;
If left entirely unchecked,
He seemed ready to destroy the nation and depart.
He seemed ready to seize all their plunder;
Ümötöy was a troublemaker,
Ready to unleash all manner of ruin.
Simply carrying out a massacre,
He seemed ready to take heads with his sword.
Striking down the mighty,
He seemed ready to leave them split beside the road.
Such was this man’s violent purpose;
The Kazakhs of Sary-Arka
Called him the warrior Ümötöy.
Good heavens, he was like a black-headed billy goat,
A slave who only barked and blustered.
He had battered against crag and stone,
A clattering brute he was.
Man, like a black camel in winter,
A snarling brute he was.
Once enraged, he spared no living soul,
Once he drank, he could not sate himself with blood.
The swaggering wretch
Never abandoned his mischief—
Ümötöy, Köksö’s son.
Ümötöy stood there working himself into a fury,
As though he would sweep all before him.
To see how fiercely he raged,
He seemed ready to end it then and there,
And carry off the Kyrgyz of Sary-Arka
As plunder.
He made his weapons ready,
And fastened on his battle gear,
Like a cloud returning with rain,
His wrath spread across his face.
He looked ready to attack,
Ready to grapple in combat,
Stepping out from the massed host,
The hair atop his head standing on end,
The hair on his face bristling,
His eyes dimmed and shimmering.
When you looked at his jaw and head,
They ground like a millstone.
Father, his strength was extraordinary,
And his valor was no small thing.
To see him in his frenzy,
He seemed able to arrive before an arrow.
If you set a man alone before him,
He seemed certain to catch and carry him off.
He was noble, and he was brave,
A truly grim, dark warrior.
The poor son of his father
Stood firmly by his word.
He had gathered an army from the Kazakhs,
And prepared himself well;
The Kazakhs of Sary-Arka
Called him Ümötöy the strongman.
He mounted the ridge with purpose,
Swaying there in proud confidence,
And stood face-to-face,
Ready to attack Choro.
God’s sun in heaven grew overcast,
And Külchoro, guarding his honor,
Was beset by sixty anxious thoughts.
His heart was torn and distracted:
“If I stiffen in anger
And thrust, my spear will surely reach him;
Ümötöy, son of Khan Köksö—
Alas, he will be crushed to dust.
Then they will say, ‘You slew your own kinsman,
You killed him for nothing.’
Renouncing the milk with which she nursed me,
Before Almighty God
And openly disowning me,
My dear mother Kanykey may say,
‘May my breast milk strike you down!’
Alas, my dear mother Kanykey—
In her anger, the unfortunate woman
Might suddenly curse me.
My dear elder Semetey
May say, ‘You attacked a foolish youngster;
What have you become, little brother?’
Man, may he not put me to shame!
He may ask, ‘How could you seize and slaughter
Our maternal cousin, our guest?
You truly are a brave man,
But what have you done
To a guest who came among your people?
He is no Chinese and no enemy,
My formidable lion Külchoro;
This deed of yours is not sane!’
Saying this, my elder
May strike me to the heart with cutting words,
And my poor soul will truly burn—
Will I be left in disgrace?
I would sooner die broken than be shamed;
Ümötöy is fierce—
I have never seen the like of him among the dead.
Without stiffening in anger,
I shall go to my khan and elder.
My silver-eyed, sun-faced,
Thunderous lion of an elder—
I shall go and seek his counsel.
Before anyone can cry, ‘Stop and turn aside!’
Saying, ‘He is your close cousin,’
In the blink of an eye
I shall tell Semetey.
If he says, ‘He truly is a Kazakh;
Leave none of his army standing,’
Then, raging to my very roots,
If the fury given me
By gracious God seizes me now,
I shall rise in wrath
And attack one of them.
I shall choose and mount a charger;
Without demeaning sword or gun,
I shall charge those accursed Kazakhs
With only a whip.
If they swarm me, I shall make them pay with their lives,
And force them to cry, ‘Mercy, dear brother!’
I shall test their vaunted courage,
